Chapter 4: Breaking Point He was eventually called to another trial, not that he ever had much say in the matter. The Fog spilled open, and Wesker moved like a blade in a shaking hand — sharp, but not steady. The cuff’s hum had threaded itself into the rhythm of his steps, each pulse tightening its hold. The first down came clumsily. Nea, screaming, kicking, was already hoisted in his grasp when the band flared red. His grip shattered open, tendons convulsing in painful stutters. She hit the ground running before he could force his body back into motion. A heartbeat later, the shockwave came — numb at first, then razor-sharp, crawling down his arm and shorting out his vision with static bursts and harsh glaring lights. By the time he blinked it clear, she was gone. And they had all noticed. Dwight body-blocked at a doorway, something he never would’ve dared before. Wesker’s lunge carried wide, nearly tripping over the man as the window missed entirely. Jake baited a strike at a pallet and ducked away a second early — timing gambled, timing won — as the wood splintered against Wesker’s shoulder. Even Claudette, usually cautious to the point of paranoia, took bolder paths. The more he missed, the more brazen they became. And when he did manage to hit, they didn’t flinch. They regrouped quickly, pulled each other up with the ease of a practiced routine. No panic. No fear. They didn’t know what was wrong. They didn’t need to. All they knew was that the killer who once carved clean through trials now moved in fits and fractures. The match ended with too many survivors upright, their laughter bleeding faint through the Fog as it closed. Wesker stood frozen in the haze, jaw tight, lungs burning. The cuff's glow sank back to its usual throb — unassuming, present, mocking. They weren’t afraid anymore. They were testing him. The next trial pushed him to the edge. By mid-match, every swing felt ragged. The static in his head came in waves now, crashing over him seemingly at random. His body staggered on inputs he never meant to send. Precision bled away in stutters. Hooks passed without use. Grabs slipped without purchase. His kills dropped. Quota dropped. The survivors began to play with him. Taunting loops. Bold saves. Close passes behind his back. Jake laughed out loud when a fully charged lunge crumpled into a twitching fall, dropping Wesker to one knee with a frustrated snarl. He abandoned the chase before the gates even fully powered up. He staggered into a deserted corridor of the realm, back braced against the wall, clutching the cuff until his knuckles went white, trying to will the world around him to settle. His breaths came harsh and uneven. Uroboros flared under the skin — eager, aggressive — but recoiled instantly as it brushed the device. The cuff answered in kind, sending a jolt down his arm that stole the strength from his legs. He dropped hard to the floor, gasping as the current burned down through his spine. His chest seized in painful staccato, breath coming shallow and uneven, rhythm knocked askew. Vision spun in swirls of too bright light that sent bursts of nausea through his core. Static crawled the walls. And somewhere, unseen, Herman marked another note. Footsteps. Too cautious to be chasing. Too slow to be fleeing. Hesitation written into the weight of each step. "...Wesker?" Shaky, soft. Open concern. Someone who knew what a stupid idea it was to come this close. Someone who should have known better but couldn’t help himself. He loitered a ways out of reach, visible only in glimpses: the gleam of glasses, the way his hands refused to lower the flashlight. The Fairfield kid. Figures. Wesker didn’t lift his head, but the tension in his frame coiled tighter. He gripped the cuff tighter, breath hissing into a low snarl. Dwight’s silhouette edged into view — half-crouched, cautious, as if approaching a wounded predator that might still bite. He hovered just down the corridor now, clearly second-guessing his life choices, but still moving forward one trembling step at a time. “You’ve been... off lately,” Dwight ventured at last. “Kind of a nice change of pace, but...you don’t seem... I just... look, are you okay?” He meant it. The idiot meant it. Wesker didn’t even need to see his face to know what that look held — sympathy. Pity. The audacity of concern. It detonated something inside him. Wesker moved before he could think, lunging across the space like a sprung trap. Dwight barely had time to gasp before he was slammed against the wall, Wesker’s hand at his throat, the other crushing down on his shoulder. "You dare to look at me like that?!" Dwight choked, hands scrabbling uselessly at the arm restraining him, boots scraping for footing against the tile, but Wesker barely noticed. The cuff’s glow flared red between them. Dwight’s gaze dropped instinctively to it — face blanching, confusion mingling with dawning fear. The cuff flared again, sparks dancing over the band, firing a pulse like a hammer blow. Wesker’s whole body jerked with it, the pain flaring down his spine and locking his joints. His grip faltered, arms twitching involuntarily. Dwight dropped to the floor, coughing as he scrambled down the hall and out of reach. Either he was extremely lucky, or something was seriously wrong. Wesker just had him, and something stronger than Wesker had forced him to let go. Wesker didn’t chase. He couldn’t. His hands spasmed uselessly at his sides, and all he could do was snarl through gritted teeth as Dwight vanished into the Fog, fear and something dangerously close to understanding in his eyes.
